newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S. says China trade with Iran honors commitments.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says China trade with Iran honors commitments.

text.p: The United States on Friday said China continues to trade with Iran, and promised to investigate new charges that Beijing may have broken commitments or laws aimed at curbing certain transactions.

But State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said there was no proof to date that China was guilty of violations, and the charges would not derail a planned exchange of summits in Washington and Beijing.

"There is no question that there is trade between China and Iran...but we have not determined that China has violated the current commitments it has made to the United States or to other members of the international community," he said.

At a news briefing, Burns did not elaborate on the China-Iran trade. But he noted that many other countries -- like Russia and many European allies -- continue to do business with Iran despite U.S. moves to get them to end any assistance that might help Tehran acquire weapons of mass destruction.

He was responding to a published report that China recently sold Iran missile technology, advanced radar components and nearly 400 tons of chemicals used to produce nerve agents. The Washington Times's story cited the Central Intelligence Agency.

The article comes ahead of a weekend meeting between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin in the Philippines and after talks in Beijing on Wednesday between U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and senior Chinese leaders that put shaky Sino-American relations on a better footing.

Christopher said China agreed to adopt a nationwide system of export controls and reaffirmed its commitment to a 1994 accord on curbing missile sales. China also pledged to seek by April 29 its ratification of the chemical weapons convention banning use, production or transfer of chemical arms, he said.

The newspaper said the alleged transfer of missile guidance components to Iran may violate Beijing's 1994 commitment to an international pact on curbing such sales. Some of the reported arms-technology transfers may violate a 1992 U.S. law requiring sanctions to be imposed on any nation exporting destabilising conventional weapons to Iran or Iraq.
Some of Beijing's commitments leave room for interpretation and for transfers of so-called "dual use" items that could be used for purposes other than weapons development.

Quoting what it called a top-secret October 2 CIA report, the Washington Times said the China Precision Engineering Department agreed in August to sell gyroscopes and other high- technology devices to Iran that could be used to build and test missile guidance components.

It also delivered in the summer nearly 400 metric tons of chemicals, including carbon sulfide used to make nerve gas, and another chemical used in producing riot-control agents and tear gas, the paper quoted the CIA report as saying.
The CIA also reported the shipment of air defence gear and about 5,000 metric tons of other military equipment, possibly to upgrade Iran's Chinese-made anti-ship missiles, it said.

Burns, citing intelligence rules, refused to say if the CIA documents were authentic. But he insisted the administration treats such allegations seriously, discusses them with Beijing and uses a variety of means to verify the facts.
